idiom_name: typed mediator class: an EventMap plus a handler registry (EventTarget/EventEmitter as plumbing)
implementation_notes: TypeScript keeps JavaScript's runtime idiom - a hub object with on/emit over a handler registry - and adds the compile-time contract that the classic Colleague hierarchy used to provide: declare an event map (interface Events { check: { checked: boolean } }) and type on/emit generically over keyof Events, so a misspelled event or payload is a compile error rather than a silently dead listener. Colleagues depend on a Mediator interface and receive the hub by injection rather than importing a module singleton, and the fan-out plumbing can be the platform EventTarget (addEventListener/dispatchEvent) or Node's EventEmitter - both string-based and untyped at the boundary, which is exactly what the typed wrapper fixes. Keep the event map as the protocol's single source of truth and create one hub per composition.
pitfalls: Types are erased at runtime, so a hub shared with untyped JavaScript can still receive an unlisted event; validate payloads at the boundary or keep the hub private to its composition.
Handlers are retained strongly and closures capture component state, so deregister on teardown (off/dispose) or the hub pins the component forever.
Unsubscribing during emit mutates the array being iterated; iterate a copy and state whether dispatch is synchronous (Node's EventEmitter and the DOM EventTarget both are).

Node's EventEmitter and DOM EventTarget are string-based at the boundary (EventTarget additionally requires a real Event object), so the typed event map is what keeps the protocol honest - strict mode cannot catch a dynamically composed event name.
